Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The Light, a new contemporary gallery opening in Durham. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian Museums See the Light: Tracey Emin and Steve McQueen illuminate Durham gallery’s revival Art of international significance planned for £17m redevelopment of museum whose closure sparked uproar Mark Brown North of England correspondent Fri 21 Aug 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Works by Tracey Emin, Steve McQueen and Olafur Eliasson have gone on display at a new contemporary art gallery and museum in north-east England which aims to show works of international significance. The Light is a £17m redevelopment of a museum in Durham that closed 10 years ago to local uproar. Then it was the Durham Light Infantry Museum and Art Gallery. Today it is just the Light, which opens to the public on Saturday with galleries on one floor telling military stories in a human and modern way, while upstairs is 500 sq metres of space for contemporary art. View image in fullscreen The Light, Durham. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian The opening is part of a bigger cultural story of getting arts and culture to places in England that have felt overlooked and forgotten. The Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art opened in Gateshead in 2002 and Mima – the venue for this year’s Turner prize – opened in Middlesbrough in 2007. They were followed by the likes of Firstsite in Colchester and the Hepworth in Wakefield. But the opening of new, publicly funded regional galleries had largely dried up, until now. Tony Guillan, who joined as artistic director three months ago, said his story played into that narrative. “I grew up on Tyneside but then left, as many people do, at the age of 18.” He worked in London at organisations including Tate and the Southbank Centre. “I always thought it would be nice to come back but there has been a dearth of opportunity. View image in fullscreen Artistic director Tony Guillan grew up on Tyneside, worked in London, and has returned to the north-east. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian “Why do you have to leave and move so far away if you want to have a certain type of career? I think perhaps more than any country in Europe we’re so centralised in London, it feels like it has far too many industries, not least the creative and cultural industries.” The development of the Light has been a long, slow process and it opens in a county where, since Labour was virtually wiped out in the 2024 local election, Reform is running the show politically. The Light is funded by Durham county council, but there is little sign in the opening exhibition that the curators are looking over their shoulders in terms of the art they are displaying. It includes works that address themes including immigration. View image in fullscreen Stuart Haygarth’s Shadey Family on show in The Light is composed of 62 vintage glass lampshades. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian Art will always have a contentious side, Guillan said. “It’s our role to create the space for dialogue. We’ve recently showed all the politicians and our corporate leadership around. They love what we’re doing. They love the ambition. They are really ambitious. So I’m very confident we’re going to have the kind of space to explore what we want to.” The curators said they wanted to show contemporary art of national and international significance. The inaugural exhibition features artists including the US artist Dan Flavin, famous for his use of fluorescent light tubes, and the Cuban-born US conceptual artist Félix González-Torres, who died in 1996, aged 38. His piece, his first use of lightbulbs, was made after the death of his partner Ross Laycock from an Aids-related illness and is about their unending love. View image in fullscreen Dan Flavin’s Untitled, 1987. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian Natasha Howes, who curated the opening show, said she had worked hard to include a good number of women and global majority artists because too many exhibitions were still dominated by white men. “Last year I was looking at a festival in Spain and I think there were 30 artists and no women. I just thought: ‘How is that allowed to happen?’” Explore more on these topics Museums Exhibitions North of England Heritage Art County Durham news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘All the watering places are crammed with hot people’: on holiday with Dickens David Shrigley London exhibition will find the funny side of old masters Missed out on tickets to see the Bayeux tapestry in London? https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5z.text: Image source, Reuters By Amy Walker Published 4 hours ago A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of carrying out a spate of sabotage attacks on Germany's electricity grid after spending several days on the run. The suspect was carrying explosives when he was detained near the Weisweiler power plant in western Germany on Tuesday, police in Cologne said. A tent in nearby undergrowth was also found to be rigged with further explosives, they added. The suspect, named by German media as Daniel V, is believed to have written letters claiming responsibility for the attacks, which have taken place in Brandenburg and Saxony in the east as well North Rhine-Westphalia in the west. Police said explosives found during the arrest were being examined by a bomb disposal expert, while officers were checking to see if any undiscovered devices had been set up in the surrounding area. Prior to the suspect's arrest on Tuesday, police said they had found several launch devices on high-voltage lines near the Weisweiler plant on Monday afternoon, alongside "another confession letter". A series of incidents across the grid in the last week have followed a similar pattern, with rockets used to shoot wires across high-voltage cables in order to cause short circuits. Image source, German police Image caption, Pictures of the suspect were released by police to German media outlets while he was on the run The attacks have led to power-generating units at some plants being temporarily taken off the grid. A statement from the Cologne Public Prosecutor's Office and Cologne Police on Tuesday did not provide further details on the suspect, or on the number and whereabouts of incidents he has been linked to. German media have previously reported receiving two letters from the suspect claiming responsibility for the attacks. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said the handwritten letters contained information that had not yet been made public. The letters were apparently signed with the first name Daniel, while his surname was kept anonymous, in line with German privacy rules. The letters also gave a residential address in the town of Gevelsberg. Cologne Police had previously said it was searching for a 48-year-old suspect from the town in connection with the sabotage of electrical substations in three German states. Investigators had also said explosives were found during a search of the suspect's apartment. In Saxony alone, police found 21 devices near high-voltage power lines last Friday and Saturday. Interior Minister Armin Schuster has admitted it could have led to a regional blackout, but he has warned against jumping to conclusions. "The way this deed was committed makes this case unusual, as well as the manner of the confession," he said. Germany’s far-right AfD party took a significant step toward exercising political power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Far-right AfD wins first state parliament speaker post To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video https://p.dw.com/p/5Nr5W Skip next section AfD will also field a deputy speaker in Saxony-Anhalt parliament 10/06/2026 October 6, 2026 AfD will also field a deputy speaker in Saxony-Anhalt parliament Mark Hallam Hans-Thomas Tillschneider has often been accused of representing the more extreme right flank of the AfD Image: Ronny Hartmann/REUTERS Parliamentarians in Saxony-Anhalt have also voted for AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider to be one of the deputy speakers in the chamber. This follows Tobias Rausch of the right-wing populist AfD being voted into the speaker's role earlier on Tuesday. Tillschneider received 44 votes in favor in Tuesday's session, while 38 parliamentarians opposed his appointment. Nobody abstained from the vote, which was by secret ballot. The AfD has 39 seats in the chamber. Lawmakers decided to elect three deputy speakers in total, with elections for the others expected to follow later. Tillschneider, aged 48, is the deputy chair of the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group. He's an AfD veteran, having joined the party in 2013 soon after it was founded. Tillschneider's known for critical views on migration and Islam, and rather less critical ones on Russia Image: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance Tillschneider is a member of the identitarian movement, and was a member of the two AfD fringe groups — the so-called Flügel (wing) and its "Patriotic Platform" — that have since been formally disbanded. He also had close ties to the Pegida and Legida groups that organized anti-migrant protests in eastern Germany. As well as his strong views on Islam and migration, Tillschneider is also known for his ties to Vladimir Putin's Russia. He was one of three AfD parliamentarians to visit Russia in September 2022, barely six months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine , in a visit that AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel rapidly disowned as a "private trip" and "not productive." Since 2023, Tillschneider has written a monthly column for the Vedomosti newspaper in Russia. He attended the 73rd birthday celebrations for Putin at the Russian Embassy in Berlin last October. https://p.dw.com/p/5Nqus Skip next section CDU state premier: Where did the votes for Rausch come from? 10/06/2026 October 6, 2026 CDU state premier: Where did the votes for Rausch come from? The outgoing premier of Saxony-Anhalt says he can't explain where an additional four votes backing the AfD's Tobias Rausch as the state's new parliamentary speaker came from. In a first for the far-right party, 35-year-old Rausch was elected to the post on Tuesday with the help of the populist BSW party (see entry below). The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group leadership had recommended that its 15 lawmakers in the state parliament abstain from voting. But CDU regional leader and current state Premier Sven Schulze said it had become clear by this morning that not all the party's lawmakers planned to do so. Some indicated that they planned to vote "no," Schulze said in comments to the German press agency DPA. "But none of us said we would vote 'yes,'" he added. "Not a single one." Rausch was elected with 48 votes in favor and 29 against from 82 eligible votes in the secret ballot. There were five abstentions. The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, meaning Rausch also got backing from members of other parties besides the AfD and BSW. The center-left Social Democrats demanded answers, with the party's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, calling for the CDU to "immediately clarify who from within its ranks may have considered this disastrous decision to be right." Klüssendorf also criticized the BSW for supporting Rausch's election. "The BSW has made a conscious decision to elect, for the first time since 1945, a politician from a far-right party to the leadership of a German parliament," Klüssendorf told the Rheinische Post newspaper. In addition to the CDU, the Social Democrats and the BSW, the Left party and the Greens are also represented in the state's parliament. The vehicle also transported other presents and documents. https://p.dw.com/p/5NqGq Skip next section Greens leader in Saxony-Anhalt says border has been crossed 10/06/2026 October 6, 2026 Greens leader in Saxony-Anhalt says border has been crossed Timothy Jones Sziborra-Seidlitz was the Greens lead candidate at September elections Image: Wolfgang Maria Weber/IMAGO The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt , Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) , Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker. The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said. "We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added. Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle." Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state." The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it. The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the party has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency in the state. Among other things, the party advocates a hard-line anti-immigration agenda and an intolerant stance toward LGBTQ+ rights. https://p.dw.com/p/5NqEO Skip next section Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker 10/06/2026 October 6, 2026 Far-right AfD candidate elected state parliamentary speaker Timothy Jones Tobias Rausch has been in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament since 2016 Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance Tobias Rausch, the far-right Alternative for Germany 's (AFD's) nomination for speaker in Saxony-Anhalt 's state parliament, has been elected with the help of the populist BSW party. Rausch gained 48 votes in favor to 29 against from 82 eligible votes. There were five abstentions. The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, giving Rausch the majority he needed to win the post, as the other parties combined — all of which reject working with the AfD — also hold 39 seats. The result, however, means that members of parties besides the AfD and BSW voted for him. Rausch, 35, thus becomes the first member of the AfD — a party classified by domestic intelligence in Saxony-Anhalt as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization — to become speaker in a state parliament in Germany. The new speaker is a real-estate entrepreneur by profession and has been a member of parliament for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt since 2016. The parliamentary session was accompanied by several anti-AfD protests in front of the parliament building. The vote for speaker is separate from that for state premier. The AfD's lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, who won the September election with 44% of the vote — thus falling short of an absolute majority — intends to stand for the position in December. As no other party so far wants to form a coalition with his party, it is still in question whether he can win a vote or form a government. The AfD says it is in dialogue with the BSW and individual parliamentarians to seek the necessary support. https://p.dw.com/p/5NpGF Skip next section EU chief warns against German-led push to cut budget 10/06/2026 October 6, 2026 EU chief warns against German-led push to cut budget Emilio Reynoso with DPA Von der Leyen urges EU states to avoid deep budget cuts Image: Pascal Bastien/AP Photo/picture alliance Ursula von der Leyen , President of the European Commission , warned on Tuesday against major cuts to the European Union's next long-term budget. "I am aware that balancing all of these constraints is not easy. I am also aware of the difficult budgetary situation in the member states," von der Leyen told the European Parliament in the French city of Strasbourg. "But I would like to caution against large cuts. They would risk undermining critical priorities that we have all agreed upon," she added. Negotiations on the long-term budget for the 2028-2034 period are currently underway. The EU's long-term budget , also known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), is the European Union's seven-year spending plan that sets how much the bloc can spend and on which priorities, such as agriculture , regional development, research, defense , migration , and climate policy . The European Commission has proposed a budget of around €1.76 trillion (about $1.98 trillion). The budget is financed mainly through contributions based on the size of member states' economies. The current MFF for 2021-2027 amounts to around €1.2 trillion. Traditionally, Germany has opposed increases to the proposed budget, while other countries favor maintaining subsidies for economically disadvantaged regions. This time has been no different, with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for major cuts. Ireland , which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, is expected to present a new compromise proposal in the coming days. European Council President Antonio Costa aims to secure an agreement on the new budget by the end of the year. https://p.dw.com/p/5NpQC Skip next section Applications to refuse military service on the rise 10/06/2026 October 6, 2026 Applications to refuse military service on the rise Timothy Jones 'We won't go to your wars' — many young people oppose Germany's new military service law Image: Lena Jakobs/dpa/picture alliance The number of applications from people wishing to refuse military service on grounds of conscience has risen sharply. Altogether 12,102 such applications were made in the first eighth months of the year, according to figures from the Federal Office for Family Affairs and Civil Society Functions (BAFzA) — more than triple the number in the whole of 2025 (3,879). The sharp increase comes after Germany's new military service law came into effect on January 1. That law foresees mandatory medical screening for young men born in 2008 or later, with an eye to recruiting volunteers to expand the armed forces. Although compulsory military service has been suspended in Germany since 2011, it remains enshrined in Germany's Basic Law. The right to refuse armed military service as a conscientious objector also remains in place. Not a compromise' Image: Mladen Antonov/AFP Advertisement Thousands of people took part in abortion-rights demonstrations across Poland on Thursday, including in the capital Warsaw and more than 20 other cities. Abortion is legal in Poland only when the pregnancy is the result of a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it endangers the life or health of the mother. As a result, most abortions are carried out secretly. The protesters held placards with slogans such as "Women's hell continues” and “Men of quality don't fear equality." Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power in 2023 after pledging to loosen Poland's abortion restrictions. But disagreements among members of his governing coalition have hampered efforts to change the law, and protesters have accused the government of breaking its promise . What is the current legal framework? Abortion has been legal in the overwhelmingly Catholic country since 1993, but only in cases involving a threat to the mother's life or health, a pregnancy resulting from rape or incest, or severe fetal abnormalities. In 2020, under the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, abortion laws were tightened even further, and abortions in cases of fetal abnormalities were banned. Activists say tens of thousands of abortions take place outside hospitals each year. Women who undergo secret abortions, for instance by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility. However, people who help them, including doctors and family members, can potentially be prosecuted and face up to three years in prison. Thousands braved the rain to call for the decriminalisation of abortion Image: Mladen Antonov/AFP Activists question government’s reform push The protests on Thursday came just days after Poland’s parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions but which are expected to be vetoed by the country’s President Karol Nawrocki, a politician with the backing of the conservative PiS opposition. "These are breadcrumbs," Kinga Jelinska, director of the Women Help Women Foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, told news agency AFP. The activists said that passing the draft laws one year before the next parliamentary election was a token gesture with no chance of passing into law. They accused the liberal Tusk government of merely creating the impression of taking action because it needed women's votes in the upcoming election.
